newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Spies pay respects to Soviet "chief terrorist".
newsitem.headline: Spies pay respects to Soviet "chief terrorist".

text.p: Russian spies past and present emerged from the shadows on Friday to pay their last respects to the man who stole U.S. plans for the atom bomb and arranged to have Stalin's rival Leon Trotsky killed with an ice pick.

The Cold War fought by Pavel Sudoplatov -- who died on Tuesday aged 89 -- is long over. But colleagues who turned up at a modest funeral ceremony in a Moscow suburb found it hard to shake off the habits of a lifetime.

One pensioner who worked with Sudoplatov gave his name in a covert whisper and one of the younger spies -- identifiable by matching macs, leather jackets and wary looks -- made one up when pressed to identify himself. "Call me Alexei," he said.
Asked about Sudoplatov's operations, which carried code-names like Stalker and Monastery, they cited the code of silence of foreign intelligence agents.
"One of the last magicians of the severe, multi-faceted, unseen front has left us," former foreign intelligence agent Yuri Oleshnikov told around 100, mainly elderly mourners.
"Thanks to his titanic and collosal work...the Soviet Union became a nuclear state in a very short time," he told the group gathered around Sudoplatov's flower-strewn open coffin.

Sudoplatov saw both sides of the brutal world of the Soviet secret services. He worked for Josef Stalin's notorious secret police chief Lavrenty Beria, who sent millions to their deaths, before being arrested five months after Stalin died in 1953.
The mourners glossed over the darker side, describing Sudoplatov's life in rose-tinted hues and condemning his 15-year jail term as the work of evil careerists.

"He loved people, he loved his department, he was noble and cultured and loved his work," said one elderly man. Asked his name, he covered his hand with his mouth. "Colonel Viktor Glazunov. He and I worked a lot together," he muttered quietly.

Glazunov said Sudoplatov was a charming and firm but fair man who never raised his voice. He was also a great one for secrecy. "He always told us not to greet each other if there was someone else there who we did not know. We just walked past".
A former World War Two partisan from Belarus said that for a long time she knew Sudoplatov only as "Comrade Andrei".
Sudoplatov's autobiography, just published in Russian, caused a storm when it came out in English two years ago.

Many scientists and historians disputed his claim that Robert Oppenheimer -- the "father" of the U.S. atomic bomb -- and his fellow scientists had leaked nuclear secrets to Moscow, allowing the Soviet Union to develop nuclear weapons.

Russia's spy chiefs, breaking their traditional silence, said there had been no direct handover of data from the scientists. In his last interview, published on Thursday, Sudoplatov said they were not agents but sources of information.

In 1953, after 32 years in the Soviet secret services, Sudoplatov was taken from his office on the seventh floor of the KGB headquarters and locked up in the basement as prisoner number eight. He was not officially rehabilitated until 1992.

The cover of his autobiography refers to him as "the Soviet Union's main diversionary and terrorist" but Sudoplatov said the interview, with the Nezavisimaya Gazeta daily, that he did not consider himself a terrorist.
Foreign intelligence spokeswoman Tatyana Samolis said you could not blame Sudoplatov without asking whether you yourself would have had the courage and will to oppose the Soviet system.
"He was a man of his times, when any task set from above was zealously fulfilled and it was not done to think about...the value of human life at all," she told Itar-Tass news agency.

Alexander Minkin, a leading investigative journalist working for the popular Moskovsky Komsomolets daily, said he had got to know Sudoplatov over the past three years and had seen documents relating to the theft of the atom bomb technology.
"I think the medals he won for his work during the war -- although not for killing Trotsky or the Ukrainian nationalists -- should be returned to his family," he said.
"I feel ashamed that today's authorities are not showing their respects here," he said, adding that the current intelligence agents were not a patch on Sudoplatov. "Maybe they are ashamed too."
